title: Ezekiel 21:28–32
context: The LORD tells Ezekiel to prophesy concerning the children of Ammon and their reproach. A sword is drawn and polished, while false visions and lying divination are spoken. Verses 30–32 call for the sword to return to its sheath and speak of judgment in the land where the addressee was created, with fire and indignation poured out until it is remembered no more. Interpreters differ on whether these closing verses address Ammon or the sword of Babylon itself, and the text can be read either way. Compare the oracles against Ammon in 25:1–7 and Jeremiah 49:1–6. Arminian and Reformed readers generally read the passage soberly as shared ground about God’s rule over every nation, including the instruments of his judgment.

verses.text: “You, son of man, prophesy and say, ‘The Lord GOD says this concerning the children of Ammon, and concerning their reproach: “A sword! A sword is drawn! It is polished for the slaughter, to cause it to devour, that it may be as lightning;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD telling Ezekiel to prophesy concerning Ammon and its reproach, with a sword drawn and polished. Ammon is not exempt.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s judgment reaching beyond Judah (compare 25:2). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as part of God’s rule over the nations.

verses.text: while they see for you false visions, while they divine lies to you, to lay you on the necks of the wicked who are deadly wounded, whose day has come in the time of the iniquity of the end.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see false visions and lying divination spoken while judgment approaches. False comfort cannot stop it from coming.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the emptiness of divination in the face of God’s purpose. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a warning against trusting false guidance.

verses.text: Cause it to return into its sheath. In the place where you were created, in the land of your birth, I will judge you.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the call for the sword to return to its sheath and judgment in the land of origin. The addressee may be Ammon or Babylon’s sword.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God judging even the instruments he uses. Readers in both traditions commonly hold the identification of the addressee with care.

verses.text: I will pour out my indignation on you. I will blow on you with the fire of my wrath. I will deliver you into the hand of brutish men, skillful to destroy.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD pouring out his indignation and handing over to destroyers. The judgment is severe and comes from God himself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s righteous anger against the nations. Both traditions commonly read the verse soberly, without dwelling on its violence.

verses.text: You will be for fuel to the fire. Your blood will be in the middle of the land. You will be remembered no more; for I, the LORD, have spoken it.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the addressee becoming fuel for the fire and remembered no more, because the LORD has spoken. His word is final.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the certainty of God’s judgment. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as the sober close of the oracle.
